privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.seoDescription: What personal data ReportAI processes, why, how long it keeps it and how to exercise your rights.
privacy.intro: This policy explains what personal data is processed when you visit this website, try the demo, write to the contact address or use ReportAI: why, for how long and what your rights are, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD).

controller.heading: Data controller
controller.intro: The controller of the data of this website and of ReportAI's accounts is:
controller.name: Owner

activities.heading: What data is processed and why

web.heading: Visiting the website
web.data: Your IP address, the date and the address requested, which the server writes to its technical logs.
web.purpose: Serving the website, keeping it secure and diagnosing errors.
web.basis: Legitimate interest in the security and operation of the service (GDPR art. 6(1)(f)).
web.retention: The logs overwrite themselves once they reach their maximum size. They are used for nothing else.

demo.heading: Trying the live demo
demo.data: The voice recording or the text you send, its transcript, the data extracted from it and the sample report. To limit the tries, also your IP address (for IPv6, only its /64 network).
demo.purpose: Showing you how ReportAI turns your visit into a report, and preventing abuse of the service.
demo.basis: Your consent, given when you send the try (GDPR art. 6(1)(a)); for the limit on tries, the legitimate interest in preventing abuse (art. 6(1)(f)).
demo.retention: 24 hours. After that, the recording, the text, the report and the record of tries are deleted.
demo.note: Please don't include real people's details: the demo is only for trying the product.

contact.heading: Writing to the contact address
contact.data: Your email address, your name if you give it, and what you tell us.
contact.basis: Legitimate interest in answering whoever writes (GDPR art. 6(1)(f)) or, if you ask about signing up, the pre-contractual steps you request (art. 6(1)(b)).
contact.retention: While the conversation lasts and, after it, only what is needed to deal with possible legal claims.

account.heading: Having an account or a free trial
account.data: Name, email, company name, your password stored irreversibly (technicians sign in without a password, through an emailed link), the version of the terms you accepted, and a security log of sign-ins and changes with the IP address.
account.purpose: Giving you access, providing the service or trial you ask for, sending the service's emails (sign-in links and notices) and protecting the accounts.
account.basis: The contract or trial you request (GDPR art. 6(1)(b)); for the security log, the legitimate interest in protecting the accounts (art. 6(1)(f)).
account.retention: While the company stays active. If it asks for deletion, the account is locked at once and everything is deleted after 30 days. The security log is kept for at most 365 days.

customerData.heading: Your company's reports
customerData.body: The data in the reports a company creates with ReportAI (recordings, photos, transcripts, reports and the details of its technicians and clients) belongs to that company, which is its controller. ReportAI processes it only on the company's behalf and following its instructions (GDPR art. 28). Recordings are deleted after 90 days, and the company can export or delete all of its data from the panel.
customerData.subjects: If you work for a company that uses ReportAI, or are one of its clients, contact that company to exercise your rights over that data. If you write to us instead, we will pass your request on to it.

recipients.heading: Who else has access to the data
recipients.intro: We don't sell or hand over data to anyone. Only the providers needed to run the service have access to it, as processors under a contract that meets GDPR article 28:
recipients.groq: transcribing recordings, in the United States.
recipients.anthropic: understanding the visit and drafting the report, in the United States.
recipients.mailgun: sending the service's emails, from its European Union region.
recipients.zoho: the contact address's mailbox, in its European Union data centres.
recipients.connectors: If a company connects its own Telegram bot or mailbox, the messages that arrive that way also go through those services, which the company itself contracts.
recipients.authorities: Beyond that, data will only be disclosed to an authority when a law requires it.

transfers.heading: Transfers outside the European Union
transfers.body: Groq and Anthropic are in the United States. That transfer relies on the European Commission's standard contractual clauses (Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914), included in their data processing agreements (GDPR art. 46(2)(c)). Neither may use the data to train its models.

automated.heading: Automated decisions
automated.body: ReportAI uses artificial intelligence to prepare the draft of each report, but makes no decisions with legal effects on you: no report is sent until a person has reviewed and confirmed it.

rights.heading: Your rights
rights.body: You can ask for access to your data, its correction or erasure and the restriction of its processing, object to it, take it with you (portability) and withdraw your consent at any time by writing to {email}. We will reply within one month at most. If you think we haven't handled your request properly, you can complain to the {authority}.

storage.heading: Cookies and storage on your device
storage.body: This website uses no analytics or advertising cookies and loads nothing from third parties. It only uses what is strictly necessary, which needs no consent (art. 22.2 of Spain's LSSI): the panel's session cookies while you are signed in, a cookie that remembers the language if you choose one (one year) and, in the field app, the phone's storage that keeps recordings waiting to upload and your profile so the app opens with no coverage. The profile is deleted when you sign out.

security.heading: Security
security.body: Data travels encrypted (HTTPS), the credentials of the services each company connects are stored encrypted, and each company can only see its own data.

changes.heading: Changes to this policy
changes.body: If anything important changes, it will be published here with its new date and, if you have an account, we will let you know by email.

architecture.heading: From audio to report, inside.
architecture.plain: What you dictate goes through five stages to become a PDF, and a person approves it before it goes out.
architecture.sub: Inside, a 25-node LangGraph graph. Pick a stage to see what it does, with what, and what leaves the server.
architecture.hintPinned: Scroll: the data moves on its own. You can also click a stage.
architecture.hintTabs: Click a stage or use the arrow keys.

dictate.name: Dictate
dictate.plain: You record the visit in the phone app, with photos if you like. With no signal, it waits on the phone and uploads on its own.
tech: The app makes the report's id before uploading and sends it as the Idempotency-Key: a retry returns the same report, never two.
The report and its queued job are created in one Postgres transaction: both exist or neither does.
Telegram and email come in the same way, deduplicated by each message's id.
dictate.why: A queue in Postgres, no Redis, no broker: one less piece to run on each client's server. Jobs are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a lease; if the worker dies, another one picks the job up.
dictate.data: The recording travels from the phone to the server. Nothing else.

transcribe.name: Transcribe
transcribe.plain: The audio becomes text, in Spanish or English, with the configured speech service.
tech: A Whisper model behind any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (/audio/transcriptions). By default, whisper-large-v3-turbo on Groq.
Temperature 0 and the report's language as a hint: repeatable output, and English audio isn't transcribed as if it were Spanish.
If the job is cut off halfway, it resumes from its last checkpoint instead of transcribing again.
transcribe.why: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint instead of a vendor SDK: switching provider means changing a URL and a key, not the code.
transcribe.data: The audio goes to the configured speech provider, with the company’s key. It is the only step that sends it.

extract.name: Fill the fields
extract.plain: The model reads the transcript and fills the template’s sections. What was not said stays empty: nothing is invented.
tech: A LangGraph graph with typed Pydantic state: each stage is a node and each decision a conditional edge.
The schema is built on the fly from the template's fields and requested from the model as structured output. Each field carries the literal quote it came from, checked against the transcript.

If validation fails, the error goes back to the model, with a retry cap. If a required detail is missing, over chat the graph pauses and asks for it; in the app it is flagged and approval stays blocked.
extract.why: Empty (null) beats invented. In a formal document, a plausible date nobody said is worse than a gap: a missing required field is asked for, never filled in.
extract.data: The transcript goes to the configured AI model (Claude or another), with the company’s key.

approve.name: You approve
approve.plain: The draft reaches the app or the chat. You confirm, correct it by voice or text, or cancel. Nothing goes out without your sign-off.
tech: The graph stops with LangGraph's interrupt() and its state is kept in Postgres: it can wait for days and survives a restart.

In the app, approving is a button that checks the required fields: nothing said or typed counts as approval. Over chat, an “ok” is settled by rules and a long reply is classified by the model; when in doubt, it's a correction.
A correction goes back to extraction with whatever was added, with a cap on attempts.
approve.why: An agent should not send anything on someone else’s behalf without a human checkpoint. Here it is an edge of the graph, not a warning in the interface.
approve.data: Approving sends nothing to the AI. Only a long chat reply goes to the model to be classified.

deliver.name: Deliver
deliver.plain: The Word template is filled and converted to PDF. It goes by email to whoever is configured, to the chat if it came from there, and stays in the history.
tech: docxtpl fills the template’s .docx with the approved fields, in an isolated Jinja2 environment with autoescaping: “Smith & Sons” does not break the document.
Gotenberg (LibreOffice) converts the .docx to PDF in a container on the server itself.
Each copy, the chat and every email, is a row in the delivery log: if one fails, only that one is retried.
deliver.why: One delivery per copy: if an email fails, the chat is not resent and the PDF is not generated again.
deliver.data: Only what is sent leaves: the PDF through the configured email and, if the report came over chat, through that chat.

topology.heading: What runs on the server and what leaves it.
topology.sub: The same containers in both modes. Only four outside services receive report data: transcription, the model, outgoing email and the connected chats.

smtp.name: Mail server
smtp.body: The PDF goes out by email through the SMTP set in the panel.
smtp.sends: The PDF and the email text, only to the configured recipients.

voice.name: Speech provider
voice.body: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Whisper on Groq by default.
voice.sends: The audio of each voice note.

model.name: AI model
model.body: Anthropic natively, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
model.sends: The transcript and the template's list of fields.

chats.name: Connected chats
chats.body: Telegram and incoming email, for whoever prefers to dictate over chat.
chats.sends: Messages, photos and the PDF, through each company's channel.

frontend.name: Panel and app
frontend.body: The office panel and the field app (PWA) in one build, with a Content-Security-Policy that uses a fresh nonce on every page.

backend.name: API
backend.body: Takes captures, messages and webhooks, and applies each request's company and role.

worker.name: Worker
worker.body: Runs each report: transcribes, extracts, pauses, renders and delivers.

postgres.name: Postgres
postgres.body: Data, job queue, graph state and usage limits. No Redis, no broker.

gotenberg.name: Gotenberg
gotenberg.body: Converts the template’s Word file to PDF with LibreOffice, without leaving the server.

storage.name: Files
storage.body: Templates, audio and PDFs, in one folder per company and per report.

keys.name: Keys
keys.body: AI, email and channel keys, encrypted in the database.

proxy.bodySaas: The way in, with automatic certificates, shared with other services on the same server.

cover.seoTitle: ReportAI, inside — case study of an AI agent in production
cover.seoDescription: How ReportAI is built: a LangGraph agent that turns a dictated site visit into the company's own Word report. Multi-tenant, with an offline field app, evals and human review. By Adrián Vázquez, AI Engineer.
cover.line1: An AI agent that writes site reports.
cover.lead: ReportAI turns what a technician dictates on a building site into their company's own Word report, ready to review and sign. I designed, built and deployed it end to end: the agent, the backend, the field app and the servers.

what.label: What it does
what.body: Voice → report in each client's own Word template. Nothing goes out until a person approves it.

hard.label: What makes it hard
hard.body: A language model that may not invent a single detail in a document someone signs. Many companies on one server, none seeing another. Recording with no signal. And AI spend with a ceiling.

proof.label: How it's proven
proof.body: 627 tests, a golden set that allows zero invented details, an independent review of major changes, public code and a live demo.

system.heading: Who uses it, what goes in, what comes out.
system.plain: A technician dictates the visit on their phone, even with no signal. ReportAI writes the report in their company's template, someone at the office reviews it, and the client gets the PDF by email.
system.mapLabel: System map: the technician dictates in the app, ReportAI transcribes and fills the template with two AI providers, the office reviews it in the panel and the client gets the PDF by email.

tech.name: Technician on site
tech.via: Phone app, or Telegram and email

dictate.name: Dictate
dictate.body: The technician records the visit in the app. With no signal, it waits on the phone and uploads on its own.

fill.name: Fill in
fill.body: The audio becomes text and a model fills the template's fields, each with the sentence it comes from.

review.name: Review
review.body: Whatever is missing is flagged. A person completes it and approves.

deliver.name: Deliver
deliver.body: The PDF comes out in the company's own Word template, to the configured recipients.

modes.title: Two ways to install it, one codebase

saas.name: Hosted
saas.body: Multi-tenant, on my server, by subscription.

self.name: On the client's server
self.body: One company, installed with one command and a setup wizard.

modes.note: One variable, SINGLE_TENANT, picks the mode. The same code and the same tests serve both.

tenancy.heading: Many companies, one codebase.
tenancy.plain: Each company sees only its own, has a ceiling on what it can spend, and can take its data away or delete it. And the same code installs, with a single company, on a client's server.

isolation.title: Isolation in code, tested route by route
isolation.body: Every route takes the company from the signed-in user, never from the request, and loads rows through one helper that filters by it. Another company's report answers 404, not 403: a 403 would confirm the id exists. A test walks the OpenAPI with two companies, tries all 29 routes with an id, and fails if a new route shows up unclassified.

spend.title: Plans and capped spend
spend.body: The quota is a count(*) over the period's reports. Every plan on sale has a daily AI spend cap, and the platform a global breaker. Every model call records its cost and tokens.

data.title: The data belongs to the company
data.body: A full export as a zip. After a deletion request there are 30 days of grace; then it is deleted in order (graph state, files, rows), so a crash halfway leaves nothing orphaned. Audio retention is configurable.

access.title: Everyone, their own access
access.body: Three office roles (admin, approver and viewer) and the technician, who only sees their own. Technicians sign in with a magic link or an 8-character code, because the app installed on an iPhone doesn't share its session with Safari, and stay signed in for 30 days with no password.

tenancy.matrixCaption: 29 routes with an id, requested by another company's admin: 29 answers of 404 and nothing changed. As a technician, 403 or 404: never a 2xx.
tenancy.why: Isolation in code rather than Postgres RLS, for now: one place to review and one test that covers it all. RLS comes with the first Enterprise client who asks for it.

fieldApp.heading: Recording where there's no signal.
fieldApp.plain: On a building site, signal comes and goes. The app records anyway, keeps the visit on the phone and uploads it on its own when the signal is back, never twice even when it retries.

record.name: Records
record.body: Opus at 32 kbps (AAC on iPhone; about 240 KB a minute), with the screen kept on by Wake Lock while it records.

queue.name: Waits on the phone
queue.body: Each capture goes to IndexedDB, tied to the session token's user rather than the profile in memory: on a shared tablet, one person's capture never uploads as someone else's.

sync.name: Uploads on its own
sync.body: When the network is back, the queue drains with a timeout sized to each upload. The report's id travels as the Idempotency-Key: a retry returns the same report.

boot.name: Opens offline
boot.body: A hand-written service worker (83 lines) keeps the app's shell. On one bar of signal, the page waits at most 4 seconds for the network, and each start-up API call 3; then the app opens with what it saved.

fieldApp.security: The same app serves a Content-Security-Policy with a fresh nonce on every page from Nuxt's own server, identical in SaaS and self-hosted. A smoke test in CI starts the built server and checks it.
fieldApp.why: A hand-written service worker rather than {'@'}vite-pwa/nuxt: the plugin had an open bug that left the manifest at 404 with our preset, and it put Workbox in the build. What we needed was under a hundred lines.

quality.heading: How I know it works.
quality.plain: “The model is usually right” isn't enough for me. Every change goes through tests, types and CI; extraction through a golden set; and major changes through an independent review.

tests.label: backend tests
tests.source: pytest against a real Postgres, on every push

frontend.label: frontend tests
frontend.source: plus a smoke test of the built server

invented.label: invented details in the golden set
invented.source: 83 cases, 3 runs: 99.8%, 100% and 99.7% of fields right

cost.label: of AI per report
cost.source: the sample report: 0.028 USD of extraction with Claude Sonnet 5, plus transcription

method.title: How I build it

spec.name: Specify
spec.body: Requirements, architecture and each task's contract: scope, interfaces and the tests it must pass.

build.name: Implement
build.body: Each on its own branch, with its tests.

review.name: Review
review.body: I read every diff. Major changes also go through a review that doesn't know my reasoning.

ci.name: Prove
ci.body: Lint, types, migrations against the models, tests, the image build and a CSP smoke test.

method.motto: AI writes much of the code. I answer for every line.

incident.title: Incident: the public demo let bursts through
incident.context: The landing's demo is anonymous and every try spends AI, so it allows 3 tries per visitor and a daily ceiling.

found.label: Found
found.body: An independent review saw that the limit was checked at the start of the request and recorded at the end, with several queries in between.

repro.label: Reproduced
repro.body: With a test: 20 simultaneous requests from one IP, 20 accepted.

cause.label: Cause
cause.body: Checking and recording were two steps, and every request saw the counter at zero.

fix.label: Fix
fix.body: One step under a Postgres lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock): each request counts once the previous one has recorded. Plus a daily AI budget of its own.

result.label: Result
result.body: The same test: exactly 3 accepted, in 6 out of 6 runs.

viz.label: Twenty simultaneous requests against a limit of 3

xss.body: A proof-of-concept XSS that went through the CSP itself: the nonce was signed with a regular expression that also signed “<script” inside an attribute. Now a tag-aware scanner signs it.

tablet.body: On a shared tablet, one technician's recording could upload under another's session. The queue is now tied to the token's user.

audio.body: A voice note sent along with text was silently dropped, on every channel. Now it is transcribed and added to the text.

revisions.heading: Revision table.
revisions.plain: The decisions that shape the system, with what they cost. Each one has a serious alternative that was turned down on purpose.

graph.decision: A LangGraph graph, not a single model call
graph.why: The flow has state and pauses: it waits for a person, asks for what's missing, retries and survives a restart.
graph.rejected: A chain of calls: every pause would be hand-written code and a restart would lose the report.

queue.why: Postgres is already there; every extra piece is operations on a client's server.
queue.rejected: Redis with Celery: more throughput than needed and one more piece to watch.

empty.why: In a document someone signs, a plausible date nobody said is worse than a gap.
empty.rejected: Letting the model fill in: more fields filled, some of them false.

onecode.decision: One codebase for SaaS and self-hosting
onecode.why: One test suite; one variable picks the mode.

rls.decision: Isolation in code, with a test matrix
rls.why: One place to review and a test that fails if a route is left out.
rls.rejected: RLS from day one: more defence in depth, with no client asking for it yet.

pwa.decision: The app (PWA) as the main channel
pwa.why: No dependence on Meta or Telegram, frictionless sign-up and review in a form.
pwa.rejected: A shared Telegram or WhatsApp bot: every company would depend on someone else's account.

login.why: No passwords on site; the code because the app installed on an iPhone doesn't share its session with Safari.

sw.why: Under a hundred lines that do exactly what is needed.
sw.rejected: {'@'}vite-pwa/nuxt: a 404 manifest with our preset, and Workbox in the build.

lock.decision: The demo's limits, in one step under a lock
lock.why: A burst gets the same tries as someone clicking one at a time.
lock.rejected: The login limiter's “may overshoot by a few”: here a burst got 20 tries through against a limit of 3.

limits.billing: It doesn't charge on its own: the plans exist, and Stripe payments are the next phase.
limits.cycle: It doesn't run the site's follow-up cycle (findings, actions and checking them at the next visit).
limits.ios: Recording with the screen locked is tested on Android, not on iPhone.
limits.rls: It isolates in code; no Postgres RLS yet.

closing.headline: If you need someone to take AI to production, let's talk.
closing.sub: ReportAI is one of my projects. The others, my experience and how I work are on my portfolio.
